title_tag: Is HomeAdvisor Worth It for Contractors? (2026)
title: HomeAdvisor: The Lead Mill the FTC Already Fined
meta: Is HomeAdvisor worth it for contractors in 2026? The honest answer: it's Angi's lead arm, it sells shared leads billed on send, and the FTC fined it up to $7.2M for misrepresenting lead quality. What to do instead.
dek: HomeAdvisor isn't a separate thing to evaluate anymore — it's Angi's lead-selling arm, running the same shared-lead, billed-on-send playbook. The difference is HomeAdvisor is the one the federal government actually fined for it. Here's the receipt.
verdict_text: For most contractors, no. HomeAdvisor (now part of Angi) sells shared leads, bills you whether the homeowner ever answers, and — this is the part no marketing blog leads with — paid the FTC up to $7.2 million to settle charges it sold contractors leads it misrepresented as high-quality. When the regulator has already written the verdict, you don't need ours. Catch your own leads instead.

blocks.html: HomeAdvisor and Angie's List merged into Angi. HomeAdvisor is the lead-generation side: homeowners request a service, and their contact info is sold — shared — to several contractors at once, billed on send. If you've read our Angi review, you already know the model. What makes HomeAdvisor worth its own page is the one fact that outranks every pricing table: the FTC.

blocks.h: The fact that ends the debate
blocks.label: On the record
blocks.claim: “High-quality leads from homeowners ready to hire.”
blocks.small: In 2023, HomeAdvisor agreed to pay the FTC up to $7.2 million to settle charges that it used deceptive tactics to sell leads to service providers — including leads that weren't for the service the contractor offered, or weren't in their area. That's not a disgruntled Reddit post. That's a federal settlement.

blocks.intro_html: The complaints line up with exactly what the FTC described:

notes.text: HomeAdvisor agreed to pay up to $7.2 million to settle FTC charges it cheated service providers with leads it misrepresented as high-quality, ready-to-hire, and matching the pro's services and area.
Shared leads, billing whether or not you respond, and charges that keep coming after you try to stop — the same complaints that followed it into Angi.

blocks.intro_html: You don't have to rent leads from a company the FTC fined. Catch the ones you already earn:
steps: Answer fast and turn on missed-call text-back (~$30/mo) so no lead slips to the next contractor.
Ask every customer for a Google review — it ranks you in the map pack, where the leads are free.
Make sure your site actually converts the traffic your truck and sign already create.
If you test any lead service, cap it hard and track close rate per source — then kill what doesn't pay.

faq.q: Is HomeAdvisor worth it for contractors in 2026?
faq.a: For most, no. HomeAdvisor is Angi's lead-selling arm and uses the same shared-lead, billed-on-send model. It also agreed to pay the FTC up to $7.2 million in 2023 to settle charges it misrepresented lead quality. Fixing your own fast call response and reviews is cheaper and more reliable.

faq.q: Why did HomeAdvisor get fined by the FTC?
faq.a: In 2023, HomeAdvisor agreed to pay up to $7.2 million to settle FTC charges that it used deceptive tactics to sell leads to service providers — including leads that weren't for the pro's service or weren't in their area, despite being marketed as high-quality and ready-to-hire.

faq.q: Is HomeAdvisor the same as Angi?
faq.a: Effectively, yes — HomeAdvisor and Angie's List merged into Angi, and HomeAdvisor is the lead-generation side of that business. The complaints and the lead model carry over.
